newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rubber - Prices range-bound, Thai outlook rosy.
newsitem.headline: Rubber - Prices range-bound, Thai outlook rosy.

text.p: Southeast Asian rubber prices are seen range-bound in thin, post-holiday trade while exporters in the world's biggest natural rubber producer in Thailand look to better times in 1997, traders said on Monday.

The long holiday in Japan, where the market was closed all of last week, and a lingering hangover from the Christmas holiday period will probably depress interest in the market until players get their bearings, the dealers said.

"I don't see anything much happening due to the holiday mood. Any possible buying is likely to be for shortcovering as players would prefer to wait and see until the market returns to normal," one Indonesian dealer in Medan said.

"Overall, prices are going to stay around these levels," a dealer for a North American rubber trading firm based in Singapore said. "There are no really strong features in the market until people shake off the effects of the holidays."
Markets around the region will also take their cue from Japan, whose markets reopen for business today, one trader said.
"Some people will be watching Japan to give some direction to the market," a dealer for a Japanese rubber trading house in Singapore said.
In Thailand, traders and industry sources said they were upbeat about the prospects for natural rubber exports in 1997 on the back of firmer demand from the U.S., China and Japan.
Thailand exported about 1.72 million tonnes of natural rubber last year compared with 1.68 million tonnes in 1995.
"Expected strong demand in Japan and China should help Thailand see another year of robust rubber exports," said a Bangkok-based trader.
The U.K.-based Economist Intelligence Unit had forecast that Japanese demand for natural rubber for 1997 will reach 676,000 tonnes compared with an estimated 670,000 tonnes in 1996.
Demand for natural rubber in the U.S. will probably reach 994,000 tonnes in 1997 and rise to 1.003 million tonnes in 1998.
"New tyre projects in China should also increase demand for rubber there," a trader said.
China's Chemical Industry News said demand for natural and synthetic rubber may reach 1.6 million tonnes in 1997.
But for some traders, strong demand in China will not translate into an immediate windfall.
"I'm not too excited by the news. Problems on letters of credit and contract defaults (are) still major concerns for Thai rubber exporters to China," one trader in Hat Yai said.
Thai rubber prices edged up slightly, mostly due to post-holiday shortcovering, dealers said.
The price of the benchmark RSS3 for February shipment was quoted around US$1.25-$1.26 a kg FOB Bangkok compared with the previous $1.24-$1.25 a kg.
Latex was quoted around $0.94-$0.95 a kg on the same basis, barely changed from last week.
Prices for Indonesia's benchmark tyre-grade SIR20 rubber are expected to move in a narrow range in the short-term with volume seen thin following the year-end holidays, dealers said.
February/March SIR20 offer prices are likely to range between 55.25-55.75 U.S. cents/lb FOB Medan, 55.00-55.50 FOB Surabaya, Padang and Palembang, and 54.75-55.25 FOB Pontianak and Jambi, they said.
February SIR20 was last traded at 55.00 cents a lb FOB Palembang and Surabaya late on Tuesday, but the quantity was small, dealers said.
One dealer in Medan said RSS1 rubber prices were still weak at 129-130 cents a kg on slow demand, adding he last sold RSS1 to European buyers at 129 cents a kg late last month.
Malaysian prices, on the other hand, may ease further this week due to ample stocks of raw materials although some consumer demand could return, traders said.
They said fine weather in late December had meant latex supply was now stable after recent shortages.
Market players are expected to return to the market after the long break but will remain cautious, traders said.
"Prices have a tendency to ease a little bit if buyers don't come in this week," a trader in Kuala Lumpur said. "There's plenty of raw materials after the improvement in the weather."

The Malaysian market has been in the doldrums since October with most institutional buyers from Europe and the United States having covered their rubber requirements until the first quarter of 1997, traders said.
But other buyers who have not covered their needs over the first three months of the year may engage in some shortcovering, they said.
"Non-traditional buyers like China, Iran and other Middle East (nations) could also be buying any time, as they're rather unpredictable," said another trader.

The Malaysian Rubber Exchange and Licensing Board quoted the benchmark RSS1 at 316 Malaysian cents a kg and SMR20 at 310.50 cents a kg, both for February buyer, at the close of trade last week. Drum latex was offered by trading houses at 240 cents a kg.
(With contributions from Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia)
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
